ObjectName.value: "Reinstated Carpet" - a finely sculptured lawn - geograph.org.uk - 1458731

Categories.value: Taken with Canon EOS 350D|Tattershall Castle (Lincolnshire)|Land art|Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland|Information field template with formatting|Images by Kate Jewell|Lawns in Lincolnshire

ImageDescription.value: "Reinstated Carpet" - a finely sculptured lawn Part of "The House of Bling" exhibition of contemporary art installations at Tattershall Castle, this intricate pattern was devised by Linda Florence, a print and textile designer turned interactive artist. She specialises in creating elaborate floor surfaces from diverse materials which are disturbed and disappear over time. This example was "painted" with builders' marker aerosols on the circular lawn in front of the castle tower and a band of local volunteers were directed by the artist to meticulously cut and close trim the pattern into the grass. Over the two weeks of the exhibition these participants have maintained the pattern. Now the exhibition has come to an end one has to ask, will these local people keep the artwork alive by continuing to maintain it or will it, as the artist intended, slowly grow out? See Mick Lobb's 1457557 showing clipping in progress half way through the exhibition.

37214745.title: File:Le pavillon de l'Azerbaïdjan (55ème Biennale de Venise) (10185595186).jpg

ObjectName.value: Le pavillon de l'Azerbaïdjan (55ème Biennale de Venise) (10185595186)

Categories.value: Rugs and carpets|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR|Photographs by Jean-Pierre Dalbéra|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation

ImageDescription.value:
Carpet Interior (détail) 2013, Œuvre de Farid Rasulov (1985-, vit et travaille à Baku) www.faridrasulov.com

Steel frame, handmade carpet, wood panels and furniture covered with carpet printed on textile; 460x690x220 cm

Titre du pavillon national d'Azerbaïdjan Ornamentation Commissario: Heydar Aliyev Foundation. Curatore: Hervé Mikaeloff. Heydar Aliyev Foundation

www.azerbaijanvenicebiennale.com


Cette installation du jeune artiste Farid Rasulov immerge le spectateur, dès son entrée dans le pavillon national de la République de l'Azerbaïdjan, dans un espace entièrement recouvert de motifs traditionnels d'un des tapis les plus connus de ce pays : le Chalabi.

L'effet est saisissant et réussi, d'abord pour le choc esthétique et visuel que produit l'installation, mais aussi pour évoquer le thème du pavillon qui est l'Ornementation et à travers elle l'identité artistique historique de l'Azerbaïdjan.

Cette abondance de couleurs et de formes met en tension la modernité de la démarche et sa part d'irrationalité avec la tradition décorative de ce pays où les tapis sont présents dans toutes les habitations.

Cette démarche n'est pas sans rappeler celle, de plus grande ampleur, de l'artiste Rudolf Stingel qui, d'avril à décembre 2013, a recouvert, des murs aux planchers, l'intérieur du Palazzo Grassi de Venise (fondation Pinault) d'un décor reproduisant des motifs d'un tapis oriental.

www.palazzograssi.it/fr/expositions/rudolf-stingel

Credit.value: Le pavillon de l'Azerbaïdjan (55ème Biennale de Venise)

Artist.value: Jean-Pierre Dalbéra from Paris, France

Label Copy: Later Mughals Installation

August 2003

Portraiture remained in demand among sub-Imperial patrons, but was generally more direct and less emblematic. This portrait is a depiction of the powerful Nawab of Avadh, Shuja ud-daulah (ruled 1754-1775), one hand on a dagger, the other on a sword. He is the ruler to whom the Mughal heir Shah Alam turned for refuge during the clash of the Marathas and the Afghans in Delhi. During the Nawabs twenty-year reign, he attracted painters and men of letters to his court, including western painters.

Westernization of style is evident in the frontal view of his face (although the body is shown in three-quarters view), the naturalistic shading in the folds of his garment, and the very deliberate, if clumsy, recession in the geometries of the carpet. There is a loss of precision in technique and an of interest in rendering visual impressions rather than complete, minute details, seen for example, in the pattern in the Nawabs slippers.

August 2008

Emerging Elites

This wealthy and powerful Nawab, lord or governor in the Urdu language, was from 1753 until 1775 a de facto independent ruler of the region known then as Awadh, a large territory in northern India essentially spanning the modern state of Uttar Pradesh. Both a patron of the arts and an able administrator, Shuja-ud-Daula maintained a vital painting atelier at his court and managed delicate political relations with the Muslim Afghans to the north, the Hindu Marathas to the west, and the British, who had gained control of Bengal to the east. Recognizing that portrait painting was a mark of prestige among Europeans, Shuja-ud-Daula invited the English academic portraitist Tilly Kettle (173586) to come to his court at Faizabad to produce oil paintings of him and his family. Indian artists in the Nawabs employ, who had been working in the imperial Mughal style, were intrigued by Kettles work and made copies on paper of his oil paintings, of which this is one example.

Tilly Kettle (Gran Bretaa, 173586), Shuja-ud-Daula, Nawab de Oudh, con su hijo, Asaf-ud-Daula. leo sobre lienzo, Faizabad, 1772. Coleccin del Muse de Versailles, no. MV. 3888.
